questions.question: What is the single abstract method of Comparator<T>?
questions.explanation: Comparator declares compare(T a, T b). compareTo belongs to Comparable.

questions.question: What does this print? List<String> c = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Rome", "Doha", "Kyiv")); c.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder()); System.out.println(c);
questions.explanation: reverseOrder() sorts by natural order in descending order, so R comes before K and K before D.

questions.question: When does thenComparing use its second comparator?
options: Only when the first comparator returns 0
Always, and it adds the two results
Only when the first comparator returns a negative value
questions.explanation: thenComparing is a tie-breaker. A non-zero result from the earlier comparator is returned at once.

questions.question: What does this print? List<String> g = new ArrayList<>(List.of("B12", "A7", "C3")); g.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)); System.out.println(g);
questions.explanation: Sorting by length puts the two-character codes first. The sort is stable, so A7 stays ahead of C3.

questions.question: list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Seat::getRow).thenComparing(Seat::getLetter).reversed()) was meant to reverse only the letters. What is wrong?
options: reversed() flips the whole chain, so rows are reversed too
Nothing, it reverses only the letters
questions.explanation: reversed() applies to the full comparator built so far. Pass Comparator.reverseOrder() to that one thenComparing instead.

questions.question: Some Traveller objects have a null miles field. Why does list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Traveller::getMiles)) throw?
options: comparing calls compareTo on the null key and throws NullPointerException
comparing does not accept method references
questions.explanation: The key comparator uses natural order, which cannot handle null. Wrap it with nullsFirst or nullsLast.

questions.question: Comparator declares both compare and equals. Why is it still a functional interface?
options: Functional interfaces may have two abstract methods
equals is inherited from Object, so it does not count
Comparator is not a functional interface
questions.explanation: Abstract methods that match public methods of Object are ignored when counting, so compare is the only one.

questions.question: Why is (a, b) -> a.getFare() - b.getFare() a risky comparator for int fares?
options: It always sorts in descending order
It needs a cast to Comparator
The subtraction can overflow and give the wrong sign
questions.explanation: Very large or opposite-sign values overflow int. Integer.compare(a.getFare(), b.getFare()) is always safe.

questions.question: Which method sorts int keys without boxing them into Integer objects?
questions.explanation: comparingInt takes a ToIntFunction and compares primitive ints, so no Integer objects are created.

questions.question: What does this print? TreeSet<String> t = new TreeSet<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER); t.add("Gate"); t.add("GATE"); System.out.println(t.size());
questions.explanation: The comparator returns 0 for Gate and GATE, so the TreeSet treats the second add as a duplicate.
